128,406 km2 (471 cells), within three cells of the gazetteer's modern Sarawak (468 cells, 118,357 km2 by cell count). Neither the Raj page nor the History page gives an area, so no ratio could be taken. Holds January to June 1946; Sarawak became a Crown colony on 1 July 1946.

region.text: 'a territory spanning from the westernmost point of Sarawak, Tanjung Datu, to the Samarahan river'

ledger.note: 1841: Brunei grants Sarawak to James Brooke, who becomes its first Rajah. 'Hashim granted Sarawak to Brooke on 24 September 1841'; 'by July 1842, his appointment was confirmed by Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II'. The History of Sarawak page gives the territory from Tanjung Datu to the Samarahan river and the confirmation on 18 September 1842.

region.text: Sarawak proper, Tanjung Datu to the Samarahan river

ledger.note: 1841: the Kuching country passes from Brunei to Brooke. 'a territory spanning from the westernmost point of Sarawak, Tanjung Datu, to the Samarahan river' (History of Sarawak). The Brunei dossier records the matching loss on 24 September 1841.

region.text: the Saribas and Skrang districts, later the Second Division (with the Batang Lupar and Sadong country the shape draws)

ledger.note: 1852: the new Sultan cedes Saribas and Skrang. 'In 1852, the new Sultan ceded the Saribas and Skrang districts, which later became the Second Division, to Brooke.' Cliopatria dates the shape to 1859.

region.text: the Rajang River basin, which became the Third Division (Cliopatria's 1868 shape also holds the Bintulu coast)

ledger.note: 1861: Brooke acquires the Rajang River basin. 'In 1861, he acquired the Rajang River basin, which subsequently became the Third Division.' Cliopatria dates the shape to 1868. The page does not name the ceding party; Brunei is read from the History of Sarawak page's Bintulu sentence.
1861: Brunei cedes Bintulu. 'In 1861, Brunei ceded the Bintulu region to James Brooke.'

region.text: the inland strip behind the Rajang and Bintulu coast that Cliopatria adds in 1870; no page names it

ledger.note: c. 1870: page silent. Cliopatria adds 95 cells in 1870 (111.1-114.7E, 1.4-4.3N); neither the Raj page nor the History of Sarawak page dates or names a gain between Bintulu (1861) and Baram (1882), so the year is Cliopatria's and the cedant (Brunei, as in the Brunei dossier) is assumed.

region.text: Baram: 'extended to 3 miles beyond the Baram River (near Miri)'

ledger.note: 1882: Sarawak reaches the Baram. 'Sarawak's territory was extended to 3 miles beyond the Baram River (near Miri).' The page does not name the ceding party; Brunei is assumed (the Brunei dossier has no 1882 loss).

1885: Brunei agrees to cede the Trusan valley. 'Brunei later agreed to cede Trusan in 1885 and Padas in 1887' (Limbang page); the History of Sarawak page has 'The Trusan river valley was ceded in 1884'. The Brunei dossier records the loss in 1885.

region.text: the Raj of Sarawak as a whole

ledger.note: 1888: Sarawak becomes a British protected state. 'Charles... secured Protected State status from them on 14 June 1888'; the Raj 'acquired protected state status... whilst avoiding cession'. The History of Sarawak page: 'Sarawak became a British protectorate in 1888, while still ruled by the Brooke dynasty'. The North Borneo page's 1888 treaty (12 May 1888) covers relations with 'the States of Brunei and of Sarawak'. Recorded on the vassal's side.

1890: Charles Brooke annexes Limbang. 'On 17 March 1890, Rajah Charles Brooke annexed Limbang', subject to British approval; in August 1892 the Straits governor decided Sarawak should keep it and pay a $6000 tribute, which the sultan refused, and in August 1895 the Colonial Office 'considered the case closed' with no agreement. The circle (25 km at 115.0E 4.75N) is the researcher's; the gazetteer lacks Limbang.

1905: Lawas is ceded to Sarawak. 'The final expansion of Sarawak occurred in 1905 when Lawas was ceded to the Brooke government.' The page does not name the cedant; the Chartered Company of North Borneo is the researcher's inference (no opened page confirms it), to be checked by the North Borneo dossier. The circle (25 km at 115.4E 4.85N) is the researcher's; the gazetteer lacks Lawas.

region.text: the interior hinterland between the Rajang and the Baram that Cliopatria's 1946 shape holds and its 1890 shape lacks

ledger.note: by 1905: page silent. The History of Sarawak page calls Lawas in 1905 the 'final expansion' but dates none of the interior (177 cells in 1946 beyond the 1890 shape). The year is read from 'final expansion'; the land may have been nominal Brooke territory earlier and the cedant is unknown ('nobody' is a placeholder).

1941: Japan invades Sarawak. Japanese forces 'landed in Miri on 16 December 1941' and 'conquered Kuching on 24 December 1941'; the Raj page's infobox gives the invasion as 16 December 1941. Sarawak 'remained part of the Empire of Japan for three years and eight months'. Recorded on the owner's side.

1945: the Japanese surrender Sarawak. 'the Japanese surrendered to the Australian forces at Labuan on 10 September 1945'; the ceremony was held at Kuching on 11 September and Sarawak went under British Military Administration until April 1946. The Raj page's infobox gives 'Allied liberation: 10 June 1945' (the Brunei Bay landings) and the war's end on 15 August 1945.

region.text: the Raj of Sarawak as a whole

ledger.note: 1946: the protected state ends with the cession. Pairs the 1888 vassal_start.

region.text: Sarawak ceded to the British government

ledger.note: 1946: Vyner Brooke cedes Sarawak to Britain. 'Sarawak became a British Crown colony on 1 July 1946'; the Raj page: Vyner 'ceded it to the British government as a Crown colony on 1 July 1946'; the cession bill 'was passed on 17 May 1946 with a narrow majority (19 versus 16 votes)'.

wars.outcome: Listed by the Raj page among the rebellions (Rentap 1853, Liu Shan Bang 1857, Syarif Masahor 1860); no territory or result is given. The History of Sarawak page mentions the defeat of an anti-Brooke faction at Mukah in 1860, which is 'not a territorial change'.

zones.text: all of Sarawak, occupied from 16-24 December 1941 to the surrender of September 1945

wars.outcome: Japan occupied all of Sarawak for three years and eight months; the Japanese surrendered on 10 September 1945 and a British Military Administration ran the land until April 1946.

certainty.note: The cessions of 1852, 1861, 1882, 1885, 1890 and 1905 were by treaty or annexation of river basins, and the pages give no survey line; the interior frontier with Dutch Borneo and North Borneo is not described on any page opened. The Limbang boundary stayed disputed after 1895 (the Colonial Office closed the case without agreement).

notes: Page budget 5 (Raj of Sarawak, History of Sarawak, Limbang, North Borneo, Charles Brooke), all used. (1) Life span: 24 September 1841 to 1 July 1946, against Cliopatria's 1842..1894 and a single 1946 shape; Cliopatria has no Sarawak shape for 1895-1945, which the 1890 and 1905 keyframes fill. (2) Cliopatria dates every gain late (1859, 1868, 1870, 1890 against the pages' 1852, 1861, 1882-1890) and folds Baram, Trusan and Limbang into one 1890 shape; the verdicts correct the years and the new 1882 and 1885 keyframes give the steps. (3) Not settled: the 1870 inland strip, the interior hinterland (177 cells) and Lawas's cedant; the Rajang basin of the Raj page and Bintulu of the History page may overlap the 1868 and 1870 shapes. The Lawas cedant 'british-north-borneo-company' is the researcher's inference, not a page; the North Borneo page is silent on Lawas and on the Sarawak boundary. (4) Counterparts: the Brunei dossier has the matching losses for 1841, 1852, 1861, 1870 and 1885 and the Limbang loss of 17 March 1890; it has no 1882 Baram loss. A British North Borneo (Chartered Company) dossier is needed for the Lawas counterpart and for Brunei's Padas/Sabah cessions. (5) The vassal pair with british-colonial-empire follows the Bulungan convention (vassal's side). (6) Sarawak joined Malaysia in 1963; a dossier for the Crown colony (1946-1963) is outside this batch. (7) Gazetteer names needed: Limbang, Lawas, Trusan (places in Sarawak; circles are used), Miri. (8) Neighbour Dutch Borneo (dutch-east-indies 1842-1894 in the seed) touches the Raj; no page opened describes the frontier.
